## The Fastest-Vanishing Landscape

Every other wilderness took ages to destroy. Forests require axes and decades; rivers require dams. Darkness can be lost in an afternoon — a strip mall goes in, a highway gets lit, and the night that reigned over that patch of ground for ten thousand years simply doesn't come back.

Ecologists have formal names for the losses they track: deforestation, desertification, eutrophication. The loss of darkness goes by mild-sounding names — skyglow, light pollution — polluted with light, of all things — but it describes a genuine disappearance. Roughly a third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Not dimmed, not obscured. Gone, the way a river is gone when you pipe it underground.

For nearly the entire run of our species, night was the default condition of the universe, and everyone knew it. The sun left, and the world was handed over. Fire, once we had it, was a small island — a ring of light a few yards across, with unbroken dark beyond it until morning. Every story humans ever told about that dark was told by firelight, with the dark audibly present, inches away, making its opinions known. The strict coastline between light and night is arguably one of the oldest things we ever thought with.

Then the timeline compresses. Oil lamps for millennia; gas lamps in the early 1800s; Edison's bulb in 1879. Within a few generations — an eyeblink — we flipped the ratio. Night went from the world's default to a curiosity you schedule, like camping. Most people now live inside a permanent, pale, humming twilight, under the underside of a light dome visible from dozens of miles away.

And here is what we forgot while conquering the dark: darkness is not an absence. It is a habitat. It has residents, economies, traffic patterns.

Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests and run toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the moonlit ocean — and now means the neon of a beachfront hotel. Generations of turtles have sprinted inland to die on asphalt, pursuing a light that was never the sea. Moths that once steered by the moon, holding it at a fixed angle the way you'd walk a straight line by a distant lighthouse, mistake porch lights for their celestial anchor and spiral obediently into the bulb. Migrating birds navigate partly by stars — experimenters proved this by putting birds in a planetarium and watching them follow the fake constellations — and on bright or overcast nights, enormous numbers collide with lit buildings. Even fireflies are running a light-based courtship system, species-specific flash patterns, and skyglow floods the signal the way a shout makes conversation impossible.

From the perspective of the night's inhabitants, what we've done is less like turning on a lamp and more like dredging a seafloor: habitat-scale destruction, conducted by the gentlest possible means.

We lost things too, though we mostly don't know to grieve them. In 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and residents reportedly called emergency services to ask about a strange, vast, silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. These were people living forty minutes from one of the world's great observatories, and the galaxy — *our* galaxy, the one containing their street and their alarmed phone call — was, to them, an unidentified object.

That used to be the one sky everyone shared. The word *galaxy* comes from the Greek for milk — the milky circle — because every Greek who ever looked up could see the pale smear. Every culture projected its rivers, animals, ancestors, and gods up there, because the sky was never blank; it was a scripture and a calendar, and it belonged to everyone the way weather does.

There are quieter costs as well. Our bodies kept the old schedule. Darkness is the signal for melatonin, the hormone that opens the gates of sleep, and electric light — blue-rich light especially — suppresses it. We read screens before bed the way a turtle reads hotel neon: as a horizon pointing somewhere wrong.

The good news is that darkness, alone among vanished landscapes, restores itself instantly. Flip a switch and it returns, exactly as it was before us. There are places set aside for it now — dark-sky sanctuaries, towns that have curfewed their own streetlights — and people drive for hours to visit, and what they report is rarely "pretty." It's more often something like vertigo. Your eyes take twenty minutes to open fully, and then the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth. And then comes the reorientation: you are not *under* the galaxy. You are *inside* it. You have been inside it the whole time. The pale band is the rest of the disc, seen from within.

I think that's what darkness does, when you let it exist — it corrects a small, constant error in how things feel. Light tells you the world is what's in front of you, human-sized and nearby. Dark tells you the truth: that the nearby is a rounding error, that the room you're in is a raft in something enormous, and that this was always so, even under the sodium lamps, even with your eyes shut.

Darkness isn't the absence of anything. It's the presence of everything else, at full volume. We ought to be more careful about drowning it out.

**The Fastest-Vanishing Landscape**

Every other wilderness took ages to destroy. Forests require axes and decades; rivers require dams. Darkness can be lost in an afternoon — a strip mall goes in, a highway gets lit, and the night that reigned there for ten thousand years simply doesn't come back.

Ecologists have formal names for the losses they track: deforestation, desertification, eutrophication. The loss of darkness they call skyglow, or light pollution, and though the phrase sounds mild — pollution of all things, polluted with light — it describes a genuine disappearance. Something like a third of humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Not obscured, not dimmed. Gone, the way a river is gone when you pipe it underground.

[Then night's history...]

For nearly the entire run of our species, night was the default condition of the universe and everyone knew it. The sun left, and the world was handed over. Fire — once we had it — was a small island: a ring of light a few yards across, and beyond it, unbroken dark until morning. Every story humans told about that dark was told by firelight, with the dark audibly present, inches away, making its opinions known. Our oldest fears and our oldest cosmologies were shaped at that border, and you could argue that the border itself — the strict coastline between light and dark — is one of the oldest things we ever thought with.

Then the timeline compresses. Candles and oil lamps for millennia; gas lamps in the early 1800s; electric arc lights in the 1870s; Edison's bulb in 1879. Within a handful of generations — an eyeblink, evolutionarily — we flipped the ratio. Night went from being the world's default to being a curiosity you schedule, like camping. Most people now live inside a permanent, pale, humming twilight. Their pupils never fully dilate. Their night sky is the underside of a light dome visible from sixty miles away.

[What darkness actually is — an ecosystem]

And here's the thing we forgot while we were busy conquering the dark: darkness is not an absence. It's a habitat. It has residents, economies, traffic patterns.

Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from nests on the beach and run for the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the moonlit ocean, and now means the neon of a beachfront hotel; entire generations of turtles have sprinted inland to die on highway asphalt, pursuing a light that was never the sea. Moths that once steered by the moon — keeping it fixed at a constant angle, the way you'd walk a straight line by a distant lighthouse — mistake porch lights for their celestial anchor and spiral obediently into the bulb, sometimes circling for hours until they die. Migrating birds navigate in part by stars (we know this because experimenters once put indigo buntings in a planetarium and the birds followed the fake constellations), and on overcast or light-polluted nights they collide with buildings by the hundreds of millions a year. Even fireflies are, in effect, running a light-based dating system — species-specific flash patterns — and skyglow floods the signal, the way a shout makes conversation impossible.

From the perspective of the night's inhabitants, what we've done is less like turning on a lamp and more like dredging the sea floor: total, habitat-scale destruction, conducted by the gentlest possible means.

[The human loss]

We lost things too, though we mostly don't know to grieve them.

In 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and some residents reportedly called emergency services and observatories to ask about a strange, vast, silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. These were people who had lived their whole lives forty minutes from one of the world's great observatories, and the galaxy — our galaxy, the one containing their street, their house, their alarmed phone call — was, to them, an unidentified object.

That used to be the one sky everyone shared. The word galaxy comes from the Greek for "milk" — galaxias kyklos, the milky circle — because every Greek who ever looked up could see the pale smear. Every culture on Earth seems to have projected its rivers, its animals, its ancestors, its gods up there, which tells you the sky was never a blank; it was a screen and a scripture and a calendar, and it belonged to everyone the way weather does. Van Gogh painted Starry Night in 1889, at the tail end of the pre-electric night, and the sky he painted is crowded and churning and unignorable in a way a modern viewer has to take on faith.

[Health + recovery]

There are quieter costs, too. Our bodies kept the ancient schedule. Darkness is the signal for melatonin, the hormone that opens the gates of sleep, and electric light — blue-rich light especially — suppresses it. We read "screens before bed" the way a turtle reads "hotel neon": as a horizon pointing somewhere wrong.

The good news is that darkness, alone among vanished landscapes, restores itself instantly. Flip a switch and it returns, the way it was before us and will be after. There are places set aside for it now — dark-sky sanctuaries, reserves where towns have curfewed their streetlights — and people drive hours to visit, and what they report is rarely "pretty." It's more often something like vertigo. You look up, your eyes take their twenty minutes to open fully, and the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth. Then comes the reorientation that ancient people must have felt as ordinary: you are not under the galaxy, you are inside it. You've been inside it the whole time. The pale band is the rest of the disc, seen from within, the way you'd see the horizon if you lived inside a plate.

[Ending]

I think that's what darkness does, when you let it exist: it corrects a small, constant error in how things feel. Light tells you the world is what's in front of you, human-sized and nearby. Dark tells you the truth — that the nearby is a rounding error, that the room you're in is a raft in something enormous, and that this was always so, even under the sodium lamps, even with your eyes shut.

Darkness isn't the absence of anything. It's the presence of everything else, at full volume. We should be more careful about drowning it out.
